title: UrbanMLLM: Joint Learning of Cross-view Imagery for Urban Understanding
one_liner: UrbanMLLM learns from paired satellite and street-view images so one model can connect city-scale layout with street-level appearance when answering urban questions.
lead: Urban understanding breaks if a model sees only one view of a city. A satellite image gives road layout, parcel structure, block density, and neighborhood context, but it misses facade detail, signage, lane markings, storefronts, and pedestrian-level appearance. A street-view image gives those local details but covers only a narrow direction from a single position. UrbanMLLM joins both views in one multimodal language model. Its core pieces are a cross-view perceiver, meaning a module that lets information from one view query and update information from the other, and a structural interleaved pre-training scheme, meaning the model reads mixed satellite, street, and text content in a consistent document order. The goal is not merely to add two image encoders. The goal is to teach the model how the two views correspond so it can reason across them.

problem.h2: Why one urban view is never enough
paras: Satellite-only systems are strong at large-scale structure because roofs, roads, water, and parcel patterns are visible from above. They are weak at details needed for human-centered urban questions, such as whether a street edge is commercial, whether there are arcades or trees along sidewalks, or how building entrances are arranged.

Street-only systems have the reverse problem. They can read local appearance, but they often do not know where that view sits inside the larger city pattern. A single street image cannot reveal whether the block is near a highway interchange, part of a dense grid, or adjacent to industrial land. UrbanMLLM tries to fuse both because many city questions require simultaneous access to large-scale context and local semantics.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Train one model on aligned satellite images, street-view images, and text so it learns direct correspondences between global layout and local urban appearance.

panels.title: 1. Satellite view gives city structure
panels.viz_args: roads, blocks, parcels, green space, water
panels.caption: The top-down view captures spatial arrangement but misses many street-level cues.

panels.title: 2. Street view gives local detail
panels.viz_args: facades, signs, sidewalks, trees, lane markings
panels.caption: The ground view captures appearance but lacks wide-area context.

panels.title: 3. Paired data aligns the two
panels.viz_args: same location -> satellite patch + street photo + text annotation
panels.caption: The dataset tells the model which views refer to the same place.

panels.title: 4. Cross-view perceiver exchanges information
panels.caption: Each view can query the other, so the model learns what top-down and street-level evidence should agree on.

panels.title: 5. Joint reasoning answers harder urban questions
panels.caption: The model can infer both what the place looks like and how it fits into the surrounding city.

steps.text: For each location, pair a satellite patch, one or more street-view images, and text annotations describing the place.

steps.b: Encode each view separately at first
steps.text: Produce visual feature sequences for the satellite image and the street image using image encoders.
Let one view query the other through the cross-view perceiver so shared evidence is highlighted and mismatched evidence is exposed.

steps.b: Arrange training inputs as urban documents
steps.text: Interleave satellite content, street content, and text in a stable order so the language model learns cross-view context over long sequences.

steps.b: Train on satellite-only, street-only, and cross-view tasks
steps.text: Use a broad task mix so the model learns each view alone and also learns when the answer requires both views together, because some tasks are solvable from one branch while others expose missing evidence unless the branches cooperate.

paras: The paper changes the interaction layer between views. Instead of concatenating satellite and street features and hoping the model discovers the relationship on its own, it introduces an explicit cross-view exchange mechanism and a training order that keeps paired evidence adjacent in context.
object.object: the connection between satellite and street-view representations

hidden.name: cross-view correspondence
paras: The hidden quantity is the location-level correspondence between what is visible from above and what is visible from the street. That correspondence is not stated in labels such as 'commercial' or 'residential' alone. It includes whether a dense roof pattern implies narrow active streets, whether a wide arterial seen from above explains the lane structure seen on the ground, and whether a green canopy in satellite view matches tree-lined sidewalks in the street view.

Learning this correspondence matters because many urban questions require translation across views. To predict a street-level property from satellite imagery, the model must know which overhead cues usually imply which ground-level cues. To interpret a street image in context, it must know what larger neighborhood pattern that image belongs to.

heat.caption: The strongest signals are the cues that connect the two views of the same place rather than cues that matter only within one view.

reads.html: The model is trying to learn what the same urban place looks like from above and from the street, and how evidence from one view should predict evidence in the other.
UrbanMLLM learns an aligned cross-view representation where satellite and street symbol positions from the same location can exchange information during pre-training and downstream reasoning.

paras: If the model only sees both views side by side, it may still solve many tasks by overusing the easier view. For example, if a label can often be guessed from street appearance alone, the satellite branch may contribute little. The cross-view perceiver counteracts that because it requires feature exchange at the representation level. A satellite feature can pull relevant street detail into its state, and a street feature can pull larger spatial context from the satellite branch.

The structural interleaving step matters for the language-model backbone because long-context multimodal models learn from sequence order. When the paired views and their text are arranged as coherent urban documents, the model repeatedly sees how global context, local context, and language descriptions co-occur. That repeated ordering sharpens the joint representation because the same place is described from several angles within one training example.

Training across satellite-only, street-only, and cross-view tasks further stabilizes the system. Single-view tasks keep each branch competent on its own. Cross-view tasks force the branches to cooperate. The result can outperform single-view systems because the model learns not just more features, but the conditions under which each feature source should dominate.

stages.s: Paired satellite patch, street photo, and urban text
Encode each image into feature sequences
Feed interleaved cross-view document to the language model
Urban answer or prediction that uses both scales of evidence

math.words: The model learns task predictions while also learning to align satellite and street features from the same location, so paired views become easier to fuse than mismatched ones.
symbols: the loss for captioning, classification, question answering, or other urban tasks
the weight on the cross-view alignment objective
the loss that encourages paired satellite and street representations to agree where they should

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a satellite patch shows a dense grid with a broad road on one edge.
The paired street image shows multi-lane traffic, storefronts, and narrow sidewalks.
If the model predicts a low-density suburban label, the task loss increases because both views contradict that answer.
If the cross-view exchange fails to connect the broad road in satellite view with the lane structure in street view, the alignment loss also increases.
A better representation links those cues, so the model can answer both 'what does this street look like?' and 'what larger urban setting is this in?'

math.note: The exact form of the alignment term can vary, but the important point is that the model is trained to reward agreement between paired views of the same location.

items.html: If a street image is weakly paired with the wrong satellite patch, the model may learn false correspondences because the training example claims two different places are the same location.
If too many tasks are solvable from one branch alone, the shared model may underuse the second branch because the easier shortcut already minimizes the loss.
Urban form changes across cities and countries, so a model trained on one data pattern may misread unfamiliar street design or building patterns unless the paired dataset is broad.
The method is strongest when the paired data is accurately aligned and the task mix includes problems that require both large-scale layout and street-level evidence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small paired dataset with a satellite patch, a street-view image, and a short description for each location. Train one baseline that concatenates both views without explicit interaction and one model with a cross-view exchange block. Include tasks such as predicting land-use type, inferring street greenery from satellite view, and inferring block density from street view.

Visualize cross-view focus weights, task accuracy, and failure cases where one branch alone is ambiguous. The demo should prove that explicit cross-view fusion changes the internal reasoning because the model uses evidence from one view to disambiguate the other.
demo.closing: The demo must show a real benefit on tasks that no single view can solve reliably by itself.
